utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. We ask the usher to have the accused brought in, please. (Accused enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would first like to know -- actually first I would like to say good morning to everybody on my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues. I would like to know whether everybody hears properly. I know there was a test done a few minutes ago so there shouldn't be any problems. Do my colleagues hear me? Is the Prosecution hearing? Does the Defence hear? Mr. Blaskic, do you hear in your own language? GENERAL BLASKIC: Good morning, your Honour. I hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am the one who didn't hear. Of course I didn't hear. I didn't have my headset on. Now we will resume our work, picking up where we left off last week. I can turn to the Prosecutor and give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours. We will proceed. Mr. Cayley will examine the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The next witness that the Prosecutor would like to call, with your permission, and if the Defence has no procedural objections, is Dr. Zoran Pajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Defence has no objection. The judges have no objection. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think first you have to take the solemn declaration that was given to you, or at least I hope it was given to you by the usher. Will you read it? Dr. Zoran Pajic (sworn) Examined by Mr. Cayley

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are a prosecution witness and it is the Prosecutor who will be asking you questions. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could you please give the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Pajic. I'm sorry. I will speak in my own language. (In interpretation): My name is Zoran Pajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give the court firstly your academic qualifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the Faculty of Law. I took a Master's Degree in Law, then acquired a Doctorate of Law, and additionally I have a special degree in psychology and pedagogy in higher education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give the court some background about yourself, professional experience, employment, professional consultancy work, university teaching and public service positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started my academic career in 1972, when I was admitted as assistant lecturer at the Law Faculty of Sarajevo, and later on, as was usual at university, I acquired the title of Professor of International Public Law at the Law Faculty in Sarajevo. In addition to teaching and scientific work that I have engaged in during the years I spent at the Sarajevo University, I was a tutor for a number of students at post-graduate level. I was also a consultant for doctoral thesis. In addition to international public law I taught related subjects such as international relations, comparative constitutional law, later on European law and European institutions. My academic career, therefore, was mainly focused on the Sarajevo University, or rather the Faculty of Law of that University, but my scope of interest led me to have contacts with all the universities in the former Yugoslavia, and also in Europe and the United States of America. In addition to teaching and research work at the University from the beginning one might say I was involved in public affairs, particularly in international law and public law in general, so that quite early on I joined in various forms of consultations in the area of law, but to leave out a period which may not be of relevance for my testimony today, I would say that my first encounter with the constitutional legal aspects of the establishment of a State and new legal orders was when I was appointed United Nations expert for South Africa. I served from 1990 until 1995 as a member of a group of experts of the United Nations for South Africa, consisting of six experts appointed in their personal capacity, and we had missions in the south of Africa, and we studied in particular violations of human rights related to apartheid and we reported on our findings to the General Assembly and the Human Rights Commission on a regular basis. On that occasion already I engaged in various analytical projects regarding constitutional amendments in the South African Republic, changes in the legislation and the introduction of new elements in the structure of the legislation of South Africa towards the end of the apartheid regime. Because of the war in my country I left Sarajevo at the end of July 1992 and until then, that is just before leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina, I kept my chair at the Faculty of Law, of course, but I was the eye witness of those turbulent events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because I was appointed -- I think that was at the very end of 1990 or the very beginning of 1991 -- when I was appointed member of the Constitutional Commission of the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was a commission for constitutional matters consisting of representatives of political parties, represented in Parliament, but a number of seats in that commission was reserved for independent experts so that four or five of us were appointed in that capacity to the Commission for Constitutional Affairs. I spent more than a year working in that commission, that is from the end of 1990/beginning of 1991 until actually the beginning of the war, because when the war began, the conditions in Sarajevo were such that that commission hardly met, and it was there that I acquired direct experience regarding the dramatic changes in the constitution and the adoption of new laws in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said that I left my country at the end of July 1992, and I came to Great Britain, where I was offered a guest lectureship at the Essex University, where I spent two years teaching at post-graduate level of the School of Law in Essex a number of subjects, such as international humanitarian law, human rights, the theory and practice, European institutions and at the time already I began to study very intensively the events in the lands emerging from the former Yugoslavia, the constitutional and legal development in those countries, the new laws that were being passed in the newly independent states that emerged from the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. At the time, of course, I took part in a large number of conferences from 1992 to the present and I'm still doing that actually, and in view of this activity of mine, and I assume also in view of my experience and my expert knowledge, I was engaged as a consultant on the part of the High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Karl Bilt, who was head of that office until recently. I was engaged on a number of occasions to express my views regarding new draft laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Specifically I participated in the drafting of the rules of procedure for the joint bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Parliamentary assembly, the presidency and the counsel of ministers. I was also consulted on a number of occasions by the High Representative in connection with legal problems that emerged in the application of the Dayton accords. Due to my interests as a professional I began studying the Dayton accords even before they were adopted, and I wrote a number of papers and held a large number of lectures at which I submitted the Dayton accords to a legal and, I might even say, a political analysis. I'm still in touch with the office of the High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina and I'm still collaborating with them. The most recent project in this area had to do with the well-known point of the Dayton accords regarding parallel relations with neighbouring states. Earlier on I was invited to brief officials at the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, which was chaired first by Messrs. Vance and Owen, and Stoltenberg and Owen. That conference met in Geneva and on several occasions I had occasion to express my views and provide consultation to the participants at this conference. A further point I should like to mention in connection with my co-operation with the High Office was a revision of the translations of the Dayton Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina in all three languages: Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian, and that publication has been officially published by the office of the High Representative a couple of months ago. As I said, I have published a number of papers linked to the Dayton accords, to the situation in the former Yugoslavia, and especially the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, I would avoid listing all those titles, but the article I recently completed and is about to be published in two very distinguished journals, one has to do with the provisions on human rights in the Dayton constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which will be published in the Human Rights Quarterly, which is a leading journal, world journal for human rights published in the United States, of course, in English, and in Croatian. This article will be published in the Collector of the Faculty of Law in Zagreb. I have just been informed that it has been admitted for publication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. I think you have established your expertise before the Tribunal. Your career and your academic qualifications and your publication are more fully set out in a curriculum vitae that you provided to me prepared in your own hand. I do not propose to admit it as an exhibit, Mr. President, but if it's of assistance to the court I will distribute copies (Handed). Professor Pajic, the Prosecutor approached you earlier this year specifically in respect of your constitutional legal expertise, and we gave you a brief on what we required of you, and I would like you to explain to the Tribunal the nature of that brief, the purpose behind it, in effect specifically what you have been asked to do and to testify to speak to before the Tribunal today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before answering Mr. Cayley's question directly, allow me as a long-standing Professor of law to express my respect for all the judges of this Tribunal for the historic mission they have been entrusted with. Ever since the Tribunal has founded I have been following with great attention and enthusiasm the work of this lofty institution of the United Nations. With the same respect and understanding I look upon the work of the Office of the Prosecutor and defence counsel, and I have deep appreciation for their contribution. Finally, I'm proud to have been shown the trust to appear as an expert witness considering this Tribunal a turning point in the history of international law. Thank you. To come back to your question, Mr. Prosecutor, by the office of the prosecution I have been asked to provide expert opinion regarding the following issues. The Prosecutor asked me to provide a detailed analysis of the legal documents of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the legal order that was established through those normative acts. Furthermore, my task was as far as possible to interpret the political goals which this legislative activity was based on to indicate the territorial aspirations that emerge from the legislation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and specifically to explain the relations between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; furthermore, the relationship between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and The Republic of Croatia of course all this on the basis of documents and regulations placed at my disposal. I was also asked to provide a clear explanation of the institutional set-up of the bodies of authority from the legal and political standpoint, to explain the division of competency and the scope of jurisdiction regarding relations between the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Defence Council. My task was also to explain the legal position of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the organisation of the judiciary, the organisation of the executive branch and, finally, to give an overall explanation of the evolution of a specific legal order that was being established within the framework of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, what did the Prosecutor provide to you in order to perform this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Prosecutor I received several volumes -- I think four or five volumes -- of the Narodni List or Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in which all the regulations passed in the period from 1992 until 1994 were published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, for the sake of the procedure of the Tribunal, could you identify the documents in front of you? Are these the documents that were provided to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those are precisely the volumes I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I can move to have these admitted into evidence now or wait for the witness to discuss them and then move to have them admitted into evidence if my learned friend, Mr. Hayman, has any comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, were these documents given to the Defence as part of disclosure of evidence or is it only today that they are being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is only today that they are being distributed, your Honour, but they are public documents. They are publicly available. They were commercially purchased by the Tribunal. They are not special documents that we have received from any particular source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not anticipate any difficulty but if we could perhaps during a break just have the opportunity to look at them to satisfy ourselves that they are authentic copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Therefore, during the break today or at another time you'll have the time to glance through them. Will they be admitted as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President. In fact, Mr. President, I can put my learned friend's mind immediately at rest. I can provide them with a copy now and also a copy to the judges and indeed English translations for the use of Mr. Hayman of extracts that have been made. I can do that now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be a good part of our proceedings with both parties here. You can give these to the Tribunal and they will be put in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards the Tribunal, for the time just give us one copy only. We do not need three. One is enough. Would you go on, please? Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, can you explain to the court the documents now in front of the judges and the Defence? Can you explain exactly what these documents are? Could you try and equate them to a similar item in another jurisdiction in order to allow the court to make an analogy, and could you also confirm to the court with foundation that they are public documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Official Gazette placed at my disposal is as a publication based on the European continental tradition where legislation and regulations were always published in official gazettes. As far as I'm aware, virtually every European state has a publication of this kind carrying laws and enactments, and the former Yugoslavia, too, accepted this tradition, so that we had an official -- a federal Official Gazette. All the Yugoslav republics had their own Official Gazettes. If we would make further comparisons with other countries, I think the Narodni List, or People's Paper, Gazette, would compare with those in other European states, like the Journal Officiel de la Republique Francaise, or the BGPL of Germany, or as far as I'm aware in the United States there is the Congressional Record of the United States. In Great Britain this publication is called Hansard and so on. So, to sum up, this is a publication which was accessible to the public and in a number of issues of this gazette you can find orders for subscriptions, an order form, giving explanations where it is published, in how many copies, who is the publisher, and in one of the issues there is a special page with Christmas greetings to all readers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now put that document before the court, I'll first of all show it to Dr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Together with my colleagues, the official journal that I was given -- this is the official journal. Was it a federal one or from one of the republics or one of the entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Official Gazette of the newly-founded entity within the framework of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The document that has just been placed before you, Dr. Pajic, is that the subscription document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is what I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This indeed supports your view that these were public documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Quite specifically this is an invitation to subscribers to subscribe to the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna so that sufficient copies may be published and orders can be addressed to the offices in Mostar, and there's a telephone and fax number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If that document could be admitted into evidence, I think that's document 36A-C. No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Pajic, in the course of your research for the Office of the Prosecutor you selected certain parts of this legislation to support your testimony. First of all, I would like to actually show you the extracts, if you can just recognise them for the purposes of production of the evidence before the court, and then if you could explain how you came to make that particular selection of documents. Dr. Pajic, if you could wait one moment while I hand out copies to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. (Pause.) Mr. Cayley, in order to speed up the distribution of these different documents, I would like to have the opinion of everybody actually, wouldn't it first be better if we were to have the witness identify the document? It is your witness. You can have the document identified. Then it's given to the Registry for numbering and then I would like to see whether it is evidence or not. I think that would be a way of speeding things you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I think that would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine so long as we are given a copy at the time the witness is given a copy, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we give the document first to the witness, who identifies it, since it's his, and you worked with the Prosecution. Then immediately it is identified by the Registrar and at the same time is given as evidence to the Defence and that is how the Tribunal will work in the future, which will not only speed things up with Professor Pajic but with the witnesses in the future. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could give copies to the Defence now, Mr. President. (Handed) Dr. Pajic, are these the documents you extracted from the purposes of your research?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a selection of the documents that I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just very briefly explain to the court, these extracted documents have been translated into English and French. The English version of the file has a grey cover and the French version has a pink cover, and the original version has a blue cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could just very briefly explain the indexing system in these files, when I refer to particular documents by number, it will be the number corresponding to the grey index down the side of the spine of the file. In document two there are a number of pages of documents and in that particular area of Dr. Pajic's testimony I will be referring to the particular page number rather than the document number. The French version is slightly longer by eight pages than the English version, so, Mr. President, I will have to give you at times a separate page number. If we can continue, Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you to the first document in the bundle, which is document 1 in everybody's file, could you explain to the court what this document purports to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allow me in a few words to inform you of the criteria I was guided by when making this selection of documents. Clearly a selection of any documents which has been reduced to maybe a quarter of the total amount of documents I had at my disposal and I was guided by the brief assigned to me by the Prosecution regarding the kind of expert opinion I would be asked to give. That is why I felt that numerous documents having to do with certain technical matters, regulating certain detailed things such as transportation, technical standards and so on, were not relevant for my testimony, and that is why I focused on these extracts that are contained in this binder. To come back to your question, the first document is the decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was passed on 18th November 1991. It is a very brief document which has a highly concise preamble saying: "On the basis of the freely expressed will of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, their democratically elected representatives at a meeting held in Grude reached the decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I refer you to Article 1 of this decision and ask you to explain the meaning of that particular decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 1 of this decision says that: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be established as a", and I underline, "political, cultural, economic and territorial whole or integrity". The meaning of this first article in my view is to round off a part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a whole, which would have certain qualities of a State.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could refer you to Article 2 of the decision, and if you could read that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 2 of this decision reads: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be composed of the following municipalities: Jajce, Kresevo, Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Kiseljak, Fojnica, Skender Vakuf (Dobratici), Kakanj, Vares, Kotor Varos, Tomislavgrad, Livno, Kupres, Bugojno, Gorni Vakuf, Prozor, Konjic, Jablanica, Posusje, Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, Grude, Ljubuski, Citluk, Capljina, Neum, Stolic and Trebinje (Ravno)". This, therefore, is a list of the municipalities which compose this territorial whole of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown Exhibit 22, which has already been admitted into evidence. If that could be place placed on the ELMO, please. Professor Pajic, if I could look at the screen in front of you, there's a map displayed which I know you have already seen. Does that accurately represent the municipalities expressly covered by Article 2 of the decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is a map illustrating what I just read out from Article 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed this is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is part of the central southern part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to Article 4 of this decision, I wondered if you could explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 4 leaves the possibility of having other municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina accede to the creation community of Herceg-Bosna provided that there is approval of the original founders of Herceg-Bosna. After familiarising you with Articles 1, 2, 3, 4 of the decision establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I wish to draw your attention to a few interesting legal aspects. First of all, I wish to say that this way of joining together municipalities which contains within itself certain elements of statehood, that is aspirations to form a State, such as political, cultural, economic and territorial whole is or rather was in contrast, in contradiction to the constitution of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which text was published in March 1993 in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Number 5. So this is the authentic text of the constitution which was in force at the time this decision was passed, of course, given the subsequent amendments, too. The constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not envisage this kind of joining together of municipalities; that is to say municipalities were not supposed to join together in order to set up independent authority in such communities, and there's another thing I wish to draw your attention to, that actually we are talking about a unilateral separation of a few municipalities into a special community. That is to say without approval or without a debate on this in the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina stipulated by the constitution in charge of that. Now I wish to draw on my legal expertise and also my Bosnian-Herzegovina background, if I may say so. I wish to say that this composition of municipalities stipulated in Article 2 is quite unclear from the point of view of national interests too, because it is a total of 30 municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, out of these 30, in 11 of the mentioned municipalities the Croat people did not even have a relative majority. So this puzzles me, I must admit, in this decision, even more so because if you look at the list of municipalities listed in Article 2, Banja Luka was left out and about one-third of the Croatian population lived there. Sarajevo was left out and I'm not sure about the exact percentages but I imagine that this could be found in documents that are accessible. About 17 or 18 of the Croat population lived in Sarajevo. So these municipalities, or rather these cities, were not part of Herceg-Bosna. So I believe that there is a certain contradiction involved here between the ethnic criterion and the territorial criterion as far as this entity of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Article 7 of this decision sets out the supreme authority or the government of this entity, this community. Could you explain that Article to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 7 is very short and it truly does not give a very clear picture as to how the government in the community will be organised. It says that: "The supreme authority of the community shall be the presidency, comprising the most senior representatives of the Croatian people and the municipality authority or President of the Croatian Democratic Union municipal boards". The only thing that is clear is that the Presidency of the Croatian Community includes only representatives of the Croatian people, that is to say only the representatives of one political party, the Croatian Democratic Union. That implies that the other nations from these municipalities were excluded from the right to political representation in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom is the document signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was signed by the participants of the meeting in Grude, as the introduction, preamble to this decision says, and here are the signatures of all the participants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. If you could very briefly refer to the final paragraphs which are in the form of preamble or paragraphs or recitals and just make a few comments to the court on those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to this document there is an explication, reasons why this decision was passed. What I wish to emphasise here is that in November 1991 Bosnia-Herzegovina was not involved in war yet; that is to say in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina war had not broken out yet, and it seems to me according to the spirit of this explanation that this is a reaction to the dramatic events taking place in Croatia, in the Republic of Croatia, rather than the jeopardy of the Croatian people in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because in this preamble they say there are divisions and grabs for other people's territories and that the Serbs were creating a so-called soukina, that they were demolishing Bosnia-Herzegovina, etc. I underline once again the fact this is November 1991, when in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no war operations yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: November of 1991 was when this decision was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 18th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. If I can now move on to document 2, and if I could bring the court's attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Judge Shahabuddeen would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, the decision recorded in document number 1 was taken on 18th November 1991. When was it published in this Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document, document number 1, the decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was not published in Narodni list, the Official Gazette, that is to say an official publication, because the Official Gazette was published only later. It started only later. What was published in Narodni List, the Official Gazette, is the amended text of the decision that I have just explained now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When was that published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The amended and definite text was published as document number 1 in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was adopted on possession of 3rd July 1992 and it was published in number 1 of the Official Gazette on 3rd July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. I understood you to be saying that the decision represented in this document was inconsistent with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina of March 1993, that is a later document. How would you explain the inconsistency of a former document with an overriding later document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I mentioned the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina I mentioned that the definite text of this constitution was published in 1993, but this decision was in contradiction to the then valid constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was valid in 1991, but it was not published for a long time, I imagine because of the war situation. So I have a copy of the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1993, when this previous constitution was published together with all the amendments that ensued, but the provisions I mentioned were valid provisions from the old constitution of 1989 amended in 1990, adopted in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Allez-y, Monsieur Procurateur.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I can take you to the next document, which is document 2 in the files before your Honours and the Defence and the document page number in the top right-hand corner is page 2. Dr. Pajic, as you have already explained, there are a great number of similarities between the previous document and this document. I wonder if you could explain to the court the significant differences between these two documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first difference that one can see is that the preamble is far more detailed of this decision or rather the definite text of this decision and this says that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a community of three constituent nations, the Muslims, Croats and Serbs, and pursuant to the general accepted principles the Croatian people established the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That is the first difference. However, from a nominative point of view the difference that seems significant to me definitely, the most significant difference, is in Article 7 of this decision. I already said that in the first decision that this was not specified in great detail what the supreme authority was. However, this Article 7 shows exactly what the structure of the government is. It says that supreme authority of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be vested in the following: the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So the post of President, the office of President, is established. Number 2, the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that's to say a collective authority, a collective organ, which now consists of the representatives of the Croat people in the municipal bodies of authority, and that the senior official there or the Presidents of the municipal Croatian Defence Council are also members. So the Croatian Democratic Union is no longer mentioned, that is to say a political party, but the Croatian Defence Council. We will see from later documents what kind of a body we are speaking of. What is very important is point two of Article 7. The presidency was given legislative function. It says explicitly that: "The presidency shall be the legislative body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you -- the date of this document, Dr. Pajic, is 18th November of 1991 and yet the decision was actually made, the amendments were made on 3rd July 1992. So this document has been backdated, has it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. It was backdated, and it truly shows continuity with the original decision, which was adopted on 18th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think another significant difference in this document compared to the previous document is that it is signed by one individual; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as opposed to the previous document, where all the participants in the meeting signed the document as mentioned, this document was signed by one person holding the office of President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was signed by Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Dr. Pajic, the preambular language, the prefatory paragraphs in this decision, would you say they are strongly secessionist in comparison to the previous decision of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the preamble is a further step in that direction, namely in having the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna leave the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and there are less elements showing that this is an entity which is still within the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. With your permission again I would like to draw your attention to Article 7, which does show an autonomous government and authority, what seems characteristic of Article 7 to my mind, speaking of supreme authority of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We see here how legislative and executive powers are brought together within the same authority, the same organ. I'm saying that because the Croatian Defence Council, which was a defence structure, now becomes part of legislative body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What is not sufficiently clear from Article 7 is that this relationship between the President as a one-man organ and the Presidency as a collective organ, one does not see whether at the same time the President is the President of the Presidency too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now move you ahead to page 4, which is the decision on the creation of the Croatian Defence Council, I wonder if you could make your comments on that particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very short document, an introductory paragraph which has the characteristics of a preamble. It says that: "The Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, faced with aggression in the territories of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the fact that the Croatian people have been left unprotected". There is no reference in this preamble whatsoever to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now we are talking about April 1992 and it was certainly faced with aggression throughout its territory. As far as the specific provisions of this decision are concerned, I wish to say that Article 1 establishes the Croatian Defence Council as the supreme defence body of the Croatian people and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the tasks of the Croatian Defence Council are spelled out in Article 2: "To take care of the sovereign place of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and to protect the Croatian people". In one opinion one already sees here clear elements of a wish for a territorial sovereignty and protecting territorial sovereignty, and I do not have to particularly emphasise the fact that this is one of the main characteristics of statehood in international law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last point, Dr. Pajic: comparing Article 7 of the previous decision on page 3 and this decision, am I right in saying that the HVO, what you have said effectively was a defensive body, becomes part of the legislature of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite explicitly. The Presidents of the municipal Croatian Defence Councils are ex officio members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which is the legislature of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now proceed on to page 5 of the documents before you, which is the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, what was the effect of this decision and what type of entity was being created as a result of this decree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority promotes the Croatian Defence Council from an exclusively defence organise into the highest, the supreme authority, executive and administrative in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So this is truly a qualitative jump, was a defence body which was founded for protecting the territorial integrity of Herceg-Bosna is now being promoted to supreme executive and administrative body. I recall that the Presidency is composed also by representatives of the Croatian Defence Council, and this shows that -- this statutory decision shows the concentration of power now in the Presidency of the Croatian Community in terms of defence and executive and administrative functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I right in saying that at this stage both the executive and the legislature was controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is an accurate assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could refer you to Article 14 of this decision, which is on page 6, could you explain that Article to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 14 and Article 15 should be looked at together, I think, for a simple reason: because they carry out in practice the principle of subordination between the National Croatian Defence Council and, if you allow me, from now on I am going to use abbreviations, instead of saying the Croatian Defence Council, I shall be saying the HVO. So it is clear from Article 14 that now. HVO supervises the work of its departments and municipal HVOs. I am quoting Article 14 now, and "the HVO may use its supervisory power to annul or abolish individual legal acts passed at municipal level". So this is the right to supervision according to the principle of subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can I have a clarification? You are talking about departments. Could you go back to number 7? What do "the chiefs of department" mean? I didn't really understand what was translated into French as "chefs du departments". I think it is 7. They talk about the composition of -- 7 says that it has "department heads". Since we are talking about that again in 14, it would be good to have clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This can be spelled out in precise terms, your Honour, if we include 20 of the statutory decision into the whole picture, because Article 20 says: "That the HVO of the HZ H-B", the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, "shall have the following departments". They are listed in Article 20. So Article 7 refers to the heads of those departments. May I continue, about your permission? This principle of subordination was heralded in Articles 14 and 15 respectively, and it says: "If for example, a municipal HVO violates the basic legal provisions of the HZ H-B, the national HVO at national level, the level of the Croat community, has the right and even duty to dissolve the said municipal HVO".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by reason of that article, the HVO was taking under its wing the complete control of the municipal government as well as the central government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is this process of centralising power in the hands of the HVO. These are the final steps, the level of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Since I have already referred to Article 20, let us be as economical as possible with our time. Let me say straightaway what this is all about. Article 20 actually establishes departments within the HVO which at first glance look like a cabinet, a government. At first glance these departments are just like ministries. That is the function they have, because I shall enumerate them, and we are talking about the following fields: Defence, the Interior, Economic Affairs, Finance, Social Affairs and finally Justice and Administration. For all these fields special departments were set up of the HVO HB and so what Article 7 says does not refer to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the HVO is part of the, or is the executive and is part of the legislature. To whom was the HVO answerable or responsible by reason of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna it was said that the HVO was responsible to the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna, and it seems to me that here we can talk about a closed circle of responsibility. On the one hand, the HVO was part of the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna. The HVO is an independent, supreme organ of executive and legislative powers, and it is responsible to the Presidency of which it is part. So from this I can draw the conclusion that this is a centralisation of power in the hands of the HVO. I'm talking about legislative functions and administrative and executive organs and defence authority, and this is now brought into question. To put it simply, there's a strict hierarchy on the basis of this decision, both of enactments and of authorities, in the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, and I can already say within the legal order of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna we see that the HVO is omnipresent in all fields of life of the Croatian Community. Then there is also a centralised structure of power from the beginning to the end, from the top to the bottom, to the municipal level, and I think that we can speak of a regime which is headed by a military organisation because, as I said at the very beginning, in the first decision the HVO was founded as a defence body. So military organisation with the prerogatives of authoritarian power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can take a pause now. The interpreters have been working since early this morning. We will resume at noon. (11.45 am) (Short break) (12.10 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. I would like to have the accused brought in, please. (Accused re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, perhaps we could have the witness that Mr. Cayley has called brought in. (Witness re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now continue and we will continue until 1 o'clock. Mr. Cayley, as soon as the witness, who I hope has rested up a little bit, is seated, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wish to make it clear for the record that in the process of my examination of Dr. Pajic I'm referring to exhibits 38A, B and C, A being the original Croatian version, B being the French version and C being the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are talking about the binders now? Is that what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I could take you to page 9 of the extract, which is the statutory decision on municipal executive authority and municipal administration, does this document show the subordination principle which you referred to earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This statutory decision in my opinion represents the final stage of the vertical structure of state institutions in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I will support this by citing Article 6, which says that: "The HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall supervise the legality of the municipal HVO's work". And then also that: "It shall instruct the municipal HVO in the field of its competence". Therefore there is a permanent responsibility for supervision over the work of the municipal bodies. Article 7 is also illustrative of what I've just said, and that is that administrative affairs within the rights and duties of the municipality shall be conducted by administrative offices, and the administrative offices shall be established by decision of the municipal HVO, which is subordinated to the national structure of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Article 7 of this decision excludes two particular offices from the municipal government and retains them within the central government. What are those two offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Article 7 provides the possibility for the municipal HVO to establish its administrative offices with the exception of the Defence office and the office of the Interior. My conclusion from this would be that these areas, the area of defence and of internal affairs, have been retained within the competence of the central organ, that is the national HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now take you to page 11, please, Dr. Pajic, this is a very short decision, but I wonder if you can briefly explain it to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By this decision the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established, known as the Narodni list of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which I have already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could now take you to page 12, which is the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, if I could make some general conclusions about this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The court is aware that I'm not an expert for military matters, but I can certainly on the basis of the legal language used in this degree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna say that this is a fully consistent legal document, and I must also add -- maybe this is the best time to say it -- that I am impressed by the clear legal language and the high level of normative activity which permeates all these documents of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or rather those published in the Official Gazette. I have studied them all and one can note a high degree of consistency. Everything is done in clear-cut legal language and it is indicative of the integralness of the legal order as it was conceived by the legislator, if I may call them that. To come back to the specific decree, it speaks mostly to the duties of citizens in the area of defence. The Defence of the independence and territorial integrity of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and without entering the military terminology which permeates this text, the text of this decision, which is quite extensive -- it has 64 Articles -- I would just say that it is clear from this decision that all the citizens of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are in one way or another in the service of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Every person according to this decree, both physical and legal entities, have their place within this system. It is clearly indicated what are the obligations and the duties, and in the end there is specific mention of legal entities, the system of command and control, mobilisation, replenishment and so on, and finally as the Crown of this whole system, there are punitive measures envisaged in the case of any violations of this decree. So this is indeed an integral document which fully covers this area of armed forces. May I specifically refer to a couple of articles? Article 3 says that: "Every citizen of the HZ H-B shall have the duty to protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the Croatian Community". This is clearly reference to statehood elements such as independence and territorial integrity, and each citizen has a different system of serving through service in the army, compulsory work service, participation in civil defence, the obligation to participate in monitoring and reporting services, and finally in certain material and financial obligations that each individual has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I can now specifically refer you to Article 7, which concerns material obligations of citizens of Herceg-Bosna, I wonder if you could explain that particular provision to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 7 of this decree says that: "All citizens of HZ H-B have material obligations consisting of surrendering their vehicles, machinery and other designated equipment". When they talk about machinery and other equipment, they probably have in mind agricultural machinery, of which there must have been plenty within the area of the Croatian Community in the households in that area: "Also surrendering of equipment and livestock for defence purposes, civil defence". It is also stated that legal entities have the same material obligation, which means that enterprises and corporations must also surrender part of their equipment and resources to meet the needs of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a unilateral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, Dr. Riad would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, the citizenship of the HZ HB is solely based on ethnic basis? When you say citizens of the HZ H-B, it means only Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't go so far as to say that, your Honour. I cannot confirm that. Nowhere where citizens are referred to, citizens of HZ H-B, is it stated that they are exclusively Croats. My interpretation is that this refers to persons residing in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In the preambles, if I may add, in the preambles of the documents on the establishment of the community, there is express emphasis on the ethnic element, because it -- reference is made to the interests of the Croatian people. I should like to remind you in view of the composition of the bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and particularly the composition of the Presidency, it is clear that only citizens of the Croat ethnicity can be members of these bodies, but when talking in general terms about the question of citizenship of Herceg-Bosna, I cannot say that this implies only to people of Croatian ethnicity, but we will come back to that in some other documents that refer more specifically to citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to supplement the question that my colleague has asked. It means that any punishments would be applied to a citizen who had declared himself to be Croatian, since there were not only Croatians in that territory. When you are talking any kind of punishment that could be meted out to individuals or companies, they would be meted out according to what criteria? They would say: "You are Croatian. You have declared yourself as a Croat". Since my colleague has asked that question, that is why this one has come to my mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The punitive provisions, certain disciplinary measures and so on, on the basis of these documents are applicable to all citizens of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I am reiterating that citizens implies persons who have residence within this territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I could just clarify Article 7, would it be correct to say it is a unilateral appropriation of civilian property by the HVO? Is that the effect of Article 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is the procedure of requisitioning material assets by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could take you to Article 23 of this decision, and I would like you to read that decision, if you could read that decision and then explain its meaning to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 23, and I quote: "In all circumstances when conducting combat operations members of the armed forces shall observe the international laws of war on humane treatment of the wounded or captured enemy, on protection of the population and other provisions of these laws". I think that this is a welcome article in a document of this kind, but it indicates again that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is attributing to itself the properties of a legal state, because only an entity that has the status of a state in international law can make statements of this kind regarding respect of international laws. A non-state or non-state community in the sense of international law could not make a statement of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now take you to Article 28 of this decision, which is on page 18, it's a short sentence, but I would be grateful if you would read it to the court, Dr. Pajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 28 says: "The Croatian language and the Latin script shall be used in the armed forces of the HZ H-B".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I believe that Article 29 of this decision sets out the command and control of the armed forces, and I wondered if you could explain to the court who is designated as the supreme commander of the armed forces of the HZ H-B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to Article 29, it is clearly stated that: "The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of HZ H-B is the President of the Presidency of Herceg-Bosna". If I may be allowed to add, however, I think this Article should be read in conjunction with Article 11 of the same degree, which says that for executing the affairs of defence, a supreme staff shall be established and the organisation of the staff shall be stipulated by the supreme commander. Therefore, the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, who will also appoint -- let me quote it: " ... who shall appoint keepers in the general staff. In the event of war a war cabinet shall be formed and the members of the war cabinet shall also be appointed by the supreme Commander", which means the President of the Croatian Community. Therefore, Article 11 and Article 29 are a whole from which we can discern the system of command of the Croatian Community in times of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, taking you back to Article 29, line 7, could you please read that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point 7 of Article 29 reads: "That the supreme commander shall appoint and dismiss from duty military commanders in accordance with special provisions".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I now take you, Dr. Pajic, to Article 32, also on page 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a very significant provision of this decision. I would like you to read it and then explain it to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Let me read Article 32: "Command in the armed forces shall be founded on the following fundamental principles: (a) unity of command and the obligation to implement the decisions and carry out the command and orders of a superior commander; (b) the commanders of the armed forces shall be responsible to their superiors for their work, command and control". I think that it clearly follows from this Article 32 that the principle of subordination has been strictly applied, as well as the command responsibility within the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now refer you to Article 34, over the page, and if you could simply read the first three lines of that Article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 34 speaks about the rights to appoint and dismiss commanders in the armed forces and says that: "The commanders are appointed as follows. The President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall appoint and dismiss commanders of brigades and high-ranking officers". Then we go one step lower: "The Croatian Defence Council shall appoint and dismiss commanders of battalions and companies as well as other officers". Finally: "Brigade commanders shall appoint and dismiss commanders of platoons, detachments and other non-commissioned officers". I think, if I may be allowed to add, that it follows from this Article 34 -- let me focus on this highest level of appointments. The President of the Presidency of the Croatian Community certainly has direct insight into all personnel appointments at the level for which he is authorised, which means at the level of commanders of brigades and higher level officers. At this lower level it is the Croatian Defence Council that appoints and dismisses commanders of battalions and companies as well as other officers. Let me just recall that the same person in the Croatian Community is the President of the HVO and the President of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I refer to you Article 37? If you would explain that provision to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very brief provision saying that the mobilisation of the armed forces shall be ordered by the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Therefore, the decision on mobilisation is within the hands of the President of this entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to Articles 43 and 44, without reading them, so that we can move as quickly as possible, if you could just briefly explain those two Articles to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These articles are important because they clearly speak of the autonomous character of the creation community, because the units of the armed forces have their own flag and coat of arms, which, as explained here, is described as the historic Croatian flag and it is described in detail in the Article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now take you to Article 63 of this decree, Dr. Pajic, this is a significant part of the decision and I wondered if you could explain that to the court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By this provision through Article 63 the provisions of the once valid law on All People's Defence are declared invalid. This was the law in the former Yugoslav Federation, the SFRY, as well as the provisions of the law on military service and that is those provisions which contravene this decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community, which means that de jure as well the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is breaking all ties with the former system of the Yugoslav People's Army. That is, I think, the substance of this Article, which was only to be expected in the transitional and final provisions of this degree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Pajic, I know you have made clear that you are not a military expert, but your general impression of this document. Would you say this is a founding document of a well organised, well structured modern army? What is your views on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The witness has stated he is not a military expert and I submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have an objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness has given an opinion. I think that it is the Prosecution that -- the Prosecution said that the witness was not an expert. You did say you were not a military expert, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness said earlier, your Honour, that although he is an expert on constitutional matters, he is not specifically an expert on matters of armed forces. I'm simply asking him to give a general opinion on the structure of the document, whether it gives certain indices of organisation, control and command, which I feel he's perfectly entitled to do and is qualified to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot grant this -- accept this objection. The Prosecutor also repeats that the witness is not a military expert and simply feels that he is asking now -- he can give a general impression which is not a military expertise. Therefore I am going to overrule the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please go ahead Dr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall briefly repeat what I said in the introduction to the analysis of this decree. My impression from the legal terminology on which this decree is based is that this is a consistent system of defence as conceived within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in all respects, in terms of the method of command, in terms of the clear principle of subordination within the armed force, in terms of responsibility, and, finally, something that may not be so noticeable at first glance is Article 62, which refers to the special rights of members of the armed forces of Croatian Community, saying that they are entitled to health care to retirement and disability insurance to child benefits and so on. Why do I consider this to be relevant? Because in the former Yugoslav people's army there was indeed a system which ensured a privileged position for the armed forces in the former Yugoslavia in the sense that members of the armed forces had their own separately organised health care service, special pensions that were calculated in a different way from those for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. If I could now refer you to page 24, which is the next decision, which is page 26 in the French translation, this is the decree on the taking over of material of the Yugoslav People' Army and the SSNO in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Dr. Pajic, what exactly is this document and what is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of this decree is what happens frequently in armed conflicts and was to be expected, that the Croatian Community would pass a decree of this kind early on, namely it appropriates the material of the JNA and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the former Yugoslavia, and I think the real word would be the expropriation of the property of the JNA and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. I have no difficulty with such a decree in principle, but what is evident at first glance is that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been excluded as a beneficiary of the resources of the JNA and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not mentioned at all as the only legitimate successor of the resources of the JNA. Therefore, this is direct expropriation of JNA material by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, bypassing entirely the legitimacy of Bosnia-Herzegovina as one of the Yugoslav republics that participated in the formation of that same JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an exercise of a State prerogative, this document or a State like prerogative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to page 26 in the Croatian and English versions and page 28 in the French version, this is the decree on confiscation of property of the occupier. This is a very similar document, I believe, to the last document that you have referred to. I wonder can you explain this document to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a certain degree of analogy between these two documents, but in this latter one it is the confiscation of the property of persons residing in countries which are defined as "occupiers" in relation to the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. It is stated explicitly here that: "Property will be confiscated of organisations and bodies of the former Federation", implying the Yugoslav Federation, "the property of enterprises and other legal entities located in Serbia and Montenegro". Then private persons, the physical entities who have the citizenship of Serbia and Montenegro and finally all those people who are nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina but who sided with what is called "the occupier" in enemy activities. So this is a wide-ranging move of a state-like nature in which private property, because this is mostly private property of private persons, is being simply confiscated and, as the Article says, becomes the property of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could refer you to page 27, which is page 29 in the French version of the translation, this is a decree on public enterprises in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Can you explain the purpose of this document and what its effect would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For those familiar with the latter day history of the economic system of the former Yugoslavia, it would be clear if I were to say that this decree is actually the ethisation of social property. I know it is difficult to explain these terms using international legal terminology, but what used to be social property, that is these public enterprises that existed in the former Yugoslavia, in this case in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is now by decreeing about the State property of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and this is being done -- let me cite a part of the Article: " ... in the interest of the economic and social development and the protection of the environment and natural resources of the Croatian and other peoples in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna". Why did I cite this? Because this is one of the few decrees among the documents that were placed at my disposal that makes no reference to war or the threat of war. So this is a State act of a peace time nature. By this act public enterprises have actually changed hands and become the property of the State. Of course "state" in quotation marks, but in any event an entity that calls itself the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and, what is more, in Article 3 reference is made to the mode of management of public enterprises, and it says that: "Public enterprises shall be managed by a management board appointed by the Croatian Defence Council". Therefore another element that we recognise in this decree testifying to an absolute centralisation and monopoly over powers, not only political powers but also economic powers within the hands of the Croatian Defence Council. Let me also refer to the areas in which this ethnisation of social enterprises was done. The production, transmission and supply of electricity, water management, forestry, mining, post, telephone and telegraph services, the railways, road traffic, areas -- information section, radio and television and special purpose industry, which traditionally in our language implies industry for wartime needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to say, Dr. Pajic, that the HVO by this decision was beginning to control every realm of life within the territory it claimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. This was a further step in terms of taking up this remaining territory which was not under the monopoly, so to speak, of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to page 29, which is page 31 in the French version, this is a decree on the law of misdemeanours. We are now dealing with specifically judicial matters, matters of the court structure. Can you explain the effects of this decision to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was speaking until now about the HVO taking over the prerogatives of the legislative, administrative and even economic authority in the sense of authority in the economic sphere of life, I did not talk about the judicial reach. This, in my opinion, is the first document, the first decree, which shows that the judiciary function was taken over by the HVO too within the HZ H-B. It says clearly in Article 4 that the misdemeanours Chamber shall exercise all powers and duties of the Republic Magistrate Court, that is the Magistrate Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So an autonomous system was being set up now of misdemeanours -- for misdemeanours in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I refer you to Article 6 of this decree? This deals with judicial appointments. Can you explain that Article to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Article is interesting because for the first time decisions or rather enactments of appointment were not passed by the HVO but rather the Presiding Judge and the judges in the misdemeanours Chamber shall, and I quote: " ... be appointed and relieved of duty by the head of the Defence department at the proposal of the head of justice and administrative department of the HZ H-B". This leads me to the conclusion that the various ministries or departments, so to speak, of the HVO which I pointed out I think in Article 20 of the decision on the establishment of the HVO as the supreme executive authority -- these lead to the conclusion that this system of responsibility in different fields by the HVO really worked in practice. So now a department or, if you wish, under quotation marks, a "Ministry", autonomously decides on appointing presiding judges and judges in the misdemeanours chamber in conjunction with the justice and administration department of the HZ H-B. So one can now really see that the HVO is working as a government, as a cabinet, and the various "ministries" discharge their duties within such a cabinet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And both of the departments that you have referred to were controlled by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were actually parts. They are actually parts of the HVO as the supreme executive authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the HVO were appointing the judiciary within this entry, within the Croatian Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, these appointments go under the name of the HVO, but concrete decisions are actually passed by the head of a certain department of the HVO as part of the executive authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I refer you to Article 11 of this decision, please? Could you read that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The dinar amount prescribed by the law in misdemeanours shall be converted into Croatian Dinars to the same nominal amount".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fining system within this court structure was specifically referring to Croatian currency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fining system is related to a currency which is the national currency of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to page 31 of your volume, that's page 31 in the English and in the Croatian version and page 33 in the French, this is a decree on the treatment of persons captured in armed fighting, could you explain this decision to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again from the point of view of international humanitarian law formally and legally this is a welcome provision, because it speaks of the fact that: "Members of the JNA and the JNA Reserve Forces and other persons captured in armed fighting against the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be treated in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Convention on the treatment of prisoners of war dated 12th August 1949".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the effect of Article 2 of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 2 of this decree implies actually that on the territory of the HZ H-B special locations where prisoners shall be kept would be set up. Special locations or centres where in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva conventions prisoners would be kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this decree make it clear who is in charge of these detention facilities or prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These prisons, as you say, are -- rather, responsibility for them is in the hands of the department for justice and administration, again in co-operation with the Defence department and the Department of the Interior. So to the best of my understanding three persons would have concurrent responsibility, that is the head of the Justice and Administration Department, the head of the Defence Department and the head of the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to Article 3, which I think goes as to control of these facilities, if you could explain that provision to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Article is quite clear. It consists of a few words only. It says that: "The Defence Department shall be in charge of the facilities stipulated in Article 2 of this decree". So the Defence Department, a special department of the HVO for defence matters, is responsible for the facilities where prisoners of war are being kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now refer you to page 32, that is page 32 in the Croatian and English versions and page 34 in the French, if you could very briefly explain this decision to the court, and give your impressions and conclusions that you drew from this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general terms I can say that this decision, together with the previous decision, or rather decree on armed forces of the HZ H-B, clearly speaks of a completed, surrounded system of armed forces, and members of these armed forces. This decision speaks of salaries and other remuneration for members of the armed forces. A certain scale is provided here in Croatian Dinars and also there are elements for paying out special benefits in the case of being wounded or in case members of the armed forces killed in action. So this is a detailed system which provides guarantees to the members of the armed forces that they would be paid for their service in the armed forces, that they will have certain security in respect of being wounded, and that their family in case of their death would be entitled to a family pension, etc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What degree of internal organisation does this indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such a decision -- again I'm speaking on the basis of the principles involved -- this could only be passed in a consistent system of organisation, firm system of organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to page 34, and again if you could just give of a brief overview of this document and the conclusions which you drew from it, this is the decision on ranks, the awarding of ranks and promotion to higher rank. This is page 36 in the French version and page 34 in the Croatian and English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Analogous to the previous decision this decision is also impressive in terms of its clarity. The elaboration of ranks, promotions, the system of promotions, the procedure according to which this is carried out in the armed forces of the HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring you specifically to Article 3, does it equate ranks in the old JNA to the new rank system in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 3 has a special function. It is supposed to make it possible to persons who had certain rank in the Yugoslav people's army to keep the ranks they had in the armed forces of the HZ H-B. That is why this provision was adopted. This is a conversion table really. I think that that is the right English word for what we find in Article 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to Article 7 of this decree, if you could just briefly explain particularly the first sentence of that Article to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first sentence of Article 7 gives the right or authority to the President of the HZ H-B to award the rank of active or reserve officer in the armed forces at the proposal of the head of the Defence Department. In my opinion, as I already mentioned, I think, in connection with the previous decision, this shows that the President of the HZ H-B did have insight and probably had the opportunity of having continuous insight as far as appointments in the armed forces were concerned related to the officers corps of the HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have come to the end of a document now and I wondered if you felt it was a convenient time to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is a good time. We will complete our work right now. We only meet in the mornings this week up to and including Thursday. The courtroom is being used for another trial. We will start tomorrow again at 10 o'clock in the morning. The hearing is adjourned. (1.00 pm)
